newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Two killed, many homeless in Bangladesh floods.
newsitem.headline: Two killed, many homeless in Bangladesh floods.

text.p: Two people were killed and more than 3,000 houses damaged as flash floods caused by torrential rains that hit southeastern Bangladesh on Thursday, officials said.
They said one child died after being swept by floodwater in Cox's Bazar district and an 18-year-old boy drowned while trying to get hold of a floating tree.

Some 20,000 people in Cox's Bazar and neighbouring areas had been moved to flood shelters, but around 400,000 others were stranded in their half-submerged homes. Witnesses told reporters hundreds of families were made homeless by the floods, set off by the heavy downpour since Tuesday.
Concern is mounting as weather forecasters predict more rain, Deputy Commissioner of Cox's Bazar, Ali Imam Majumder, said.
"The monsoon is very active this year. We expect many showers in the next few days," one meteorology official in Chittagong said.
Many rivers in the area have burst their banks, flooding villages and sweeping away a bridge on the highway between Chittagong port and Cox's Bazar.
Civil aviation officials said Bangladesh national airline Biman had suspended or delayed flights to Chittagong and Cox's Bazar.
Cargo handling at the Chittagong port has also been hampered.
The flooding has hit areas in the country which were still recovering from a severe cyclone on May 19 that killed over 100 people and injured thousands.
Heavy rain also hit Chittagong Hill Tracts, where tribal rebels have been fighting for autonomy over last 23 years, local officials said.
"Worst hit is the Bandarban district (in the Hill Tracts) where more than 1,000 thatched houses have been washed down the hills," one official told reporters.
People have been warned of possible landslides, he said without giving details.
Transport operators said road communication between Chittagong and Bandarban was cut on Thursday afternoon.
Heavy rain has also hit the Bangladesh capital Dhaka, a city of nine million people, a quarter of whom live in slums.
